sections.body: The source targets one-bounce direct lighting from many dynamic emissive surfaces under real-time ray budgets. It treats the problem as hard even for offline renderers because important lights depend jointly on visibility, BSDF response, geometry, and emitted power, while interactive applications cannot afford exhaustive shadow rays or heavy per-frame structures.
sections.heading: Problem Setting

sections.body: ReSTIR uses weighted reservoir sampling to keep a compact state per pixel: a selected light sample, accumulated weight information, and the number of candidates represented. Reservoirs can then be combined without recovering their original streams, letting spatial neighbors and previous frames contribute candidate information at low storage cost.
sections.heading: Reservoir Reuse Mechanism

sections.body: The paper is explicit that naive spatiotemporal reuse mixes different pixel distributions and can introduce bias. Its analysis shows how modified RIS weights and MIS-style balancing can preserve unbiasedness, but the practical unbiased path can require extra visibility tests. The biased path is cheaper and lower variance but may darken difficult boundaries.
sections.heading: Biased And Unbiased Modes

sections.body: The reported measurements connect the math to GPU rendering. The abstract gives equal-error speedups of 6x-60x for the unbiased estimator and 35x-65x for the biased estimator, while figure captions report real-time images at 1920 x 1080 with 11,000 and 3.4 million dynamic emissive triangles.
sections.heading: Performance Evidence

sections.body: ReSTIR is positioned as complementary to denoising rather than a replacement for it. The paper argues that denoisers cannot restore features missing from their input samples, so improving sample quality inside the renderer can make the denoiser's later reconstruction task better conditioned.
sections.heading: Denoising Interpretation

sections.body: The approach relies on spatial and temporal sample relevance. It is less effective around disocclusions, lighting discontinuities, fast moving lights, and high geometric complexity. Because the implementation stores reservoirs in image buffers, its demonstrated scope is primary-hit direct lighting rather than arbitrary deeper-path global illumination.
sections.heading: Assumptions And Limits

source_dossier.summary_long: This paper introduces ReSTIR, Reservoir-based Spatio-Temporal Importance Resampling, for real-time ray-traced direct lighting with many dynamic emitters. The core problem is that a renderer cannot trace shadow rays to all lights, and in real-time settings it may only afford a few rays per pixel. ReSTIR addresses that constraint by generating a small set of per-pixel light candidates, resampling them with a target distribution based on unshadowed path contribution, and storing only the selected sample, its weight, and the effective candidate count in a reservoir. The key algorithmic move is that reservoirs can be combined as if their original candidate streams had been concatenated, which lets nearby pixels and prior frames share useful sampling information without storing every candidate. This turns spatial and temporal coherence into better sampling PDFs inside the renderer rather than post-process filtering of colors. The paper also analyzes why naive reuse across pixels can introduce bias: neighboring pixels may have different target distributions, visibility, normals, and supports. It derives an unbiased correction using modified RIS weights and multiple-importance-style candidate-PDF weights, but notes that visibility-aware unbiased reuse can require additional shadow rays. As a result, the implementation offers both biased and unbiased variants. The biased version is faster and often lower variance at interactive budgets, but it can darken difficult regions such as shadow boundaries, highlights, or complex geometry. The reported results are substantial: the abstract claims equal-error speedups of 6x-60x for the unbiased estimator and 35x-65x for the biased estimator, and figures show scenes with 11,000 to 3.4 million dynamic emissive triangles rendered at 1920 x 1080 in tens of milliseconds. The method is strongest as a first-hit direct-lighting technique in scenes where neighboring pixels and previous frames provide relevant samples. It is weaker near disocclusions, fast moving lights, lighting discontinuities, and cases where image-space correlation breaks down; extending it beyond primary-hit direct lighting remains future work.
source_dossier.summary_short: ReSTIR treats real-time many-light direct illumination as a reservoir resampling problem. It stores compact per-pixel reservoirs, reuses selected candidates across neighbors and prior frames, and offers biased and unbiased modes. The result is fast GPU rendering with clear limits around discontinuities, weak correlation, and first-hit image-space scope.

source_semantic.display_title: ReSTIR Makes Dynamic Direct Lighting Real-Time

summary: ReSTIR is a reservoir-based Monte Carlo method for real-time direct lighting from many dynamic emitters. It reuses light samples across pixels and frames, offers biased and unbiased variants, and reports large equal-error speedups on GPU scenes with thousands to millions of emissive triangles. Its main tradeoffs are bias and darkening in the cheaper mode, extra ray cost in the unbiased mode, and reduced benefit where image-space spatiotemporal correlation is weak.
title: Spatiotemporal Reservoir Resampling for Real-Time Ray Tracing with Dynamic Direct Lighting
